title: Can a Grid Trading Bot Really Generate Consistent Profits?
author: Wide_Charge_8599
selftext:
​

I've been running a grid trading bot and want to share my current results.

💰 Investment: $23,582

📈 Monthly Profit: $1,038

📊 Monthly Return: 4.40%

🚀 Annualized Return: 52.82% (simple projection)

The results look promising, but can these returns be sustained over the long term?

For experienced grid bot traders:

\- What monthly returns do you typically achieve?

\- How do you manage strong market trends and unrealized losses?

\- Can grid trading remain profitable in the long run?

I'd love to hear your real-world experiences, including failures and lessons learned!

comments.author: Scott_Malkinsons
comments.body:
Grids can definitely work, but going by your returns I'm pretty sure you're doing the "bad" grid type which will eventually bite you in the ass.

You're taking say 1 lot, then taking another lot if price goes against you, and so forth. Grids work just fine if you say your max risk is say 1 lot (1-2% of account or so) and then you divide it up. So you go in with 0.1 lot, and then another 0.1 so you get a better average entry.

The flaw is you'll probably not get to full 1 lot very often if you're entries are somewhat accurate and the grid isn't super tight. So it's entirely possible that grid actually makes less money. For most people, grid is just doing things more complicated for little extra return (unless you, like I suspect you're doing, is a grid with martingale. That works, until it doesn't).

I also like how you seem to have, conveniently?, forgotten entirely about your unrealized loss being -4,961. What's your plan here? Hold indefinitely? Because if you close your positions right now, you'd be well in the negative. So I have no idea why the heck you're "advertising yourself" as having made a profit with a promising strategy. You haven't made shit. And you SURE AF aren't projected to make 52% this year. You're projected to lose your ass.

replies.author: Wide_Charge_8599
replies.body: My strategy involves entering positions with $8 to $25 each, using a total capital of $23,578. The plan is to hold these positions indefinitely—for 3, 5, or even 10 years—without closing them out. I also maintain both long and short positions. What do you think of this strategy?

replies.author: Shoddy_Peanut7320
replies.body: Honest answer: a plan to hold indefinitely only works if the account can survive the worst move without liquidation, so I’d define a maximum loss and the exit rule in advance and count funding on every position. The strategy then needs an annualised return on equity after unrealized losses, tracked over a long enough period to include a trend against it. A projection from one month of realized profit isn’t a forecast of the next year

replies.author: Wide_Charge_8599
replies.body: That’s right; I set the leverage to 1x and enter long or short positions. In the case of short positions, you may actually need to add to your margin balance to avoid liquidation. I have also been running and testing grid bots for about three years now. Since the platform supports a virtual mode, you can run simulated tests as well.

replies.author: Shoddy_Peanut7320
replies.body: Running at 1x helps with liquidation on the long side, but shorts have no price ceiling, so the margin you'd need to add is open-ended, and funding costs on perps keep accruing on both sides. I'd track the return on total equity, including unrealized losses and every margin top-up, over the three years you've run it, and compare that with simply holding the same coins. Virtual mode is a good place to replay a hard trending stretch before adding real money.

comments.author: tradematesHQ
comments.body: 4.40% monthly annualized to 52.82% is the tell, that's not sustainable. Grids print in chop and bleed in trends, so the real question is how much unrealized loss you're sitting on when the market runs.

replies.author: Wide_Charge_8599
replies.body: Yes, that's right; I'm trying out "infinite trading"—setting it up so that the grid operates across all price ranges. I am still in the testing phase, though.

comments.author: Shoddy_Peanut7320
comments.body: Hold-forever grids with long and short legs can look consistent because realized profits accumulate while losses stay unrealized, so the number to watch is the margin balance, not realized P&L. In the screenshot the unrealized loss is about -4,691 USDT against a margin balance of 18,900, so the account is below its starting capital, and the monthly return should be quoted on equity. A realistic test is to replay the same grid on historical data including a strong one-way trend (for example a 40% drop or rally) and see the maximum drawdown and margin usage, plus funding costs on perps, which accumulate on positions held for years. Funding Rate Radar at Cymetica shows perp funding side by side across venues, which is one way to estimate that holding cost.

replies.author: Wide_Charge_8599
replies.body:
That’s right; with altcoins, you often have to hold through gains of more than 10x. The funding rate has remained at a healthy level over the past year.

The same page shows the net profit/loss over that period at about -$3,115, so the figure that matters for the grid is that realized result together with the unrealized loss, counted on your equity.
